Name: Day 01: The security mindset, CIA and AAA
Outcome: Explain confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization and accounting with a real example of each.
Lab: Clone this repo and create notes/day-01.md from notes/TEMPLATE.md. | Pick a system you ran in DevOps (for example a CI server or a production API). | For that system write one way an attacker could break C, I and A, and one control that stops each. | Add which AAA control is in place today (SSO? audit logs?) and which is missing.
SME Question: A product manager asks: 'We encrypt everything, so we are secure, right?' Answer in 60 seconds using CIA.

Name: Day 02: Threats, vulnerabilities, risk and controls
Outcome: Define threat, vulnerability, exploit, risk and impact precisely, and classify controls by type and function.
Lab: Build a 5-row risk register for a CI/CD pipeline in a markdown table. | Columns: asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood (1-5), impact (1-5), risk score, control, control type (preventive/detective/corrective). | Include at least one supply-chain risk (for example a compromised dependency) and one insider risk.
SME Question: What is the difference between a threat, a vulnerability and a risk? Give an example from a Kubernetes cluster.

Name: Day 03: Security frameworks, NIST CSF 2.0 and CIS Controls
Outcome: Name the six NIST CSF 2.0 functions and explain how CIS Controls and ISO 27001 relate to it.
Lab: Draw a table with the six CSF functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). | Map at least two things you did in DevOps to each function (for example backups map to Recover, alerting to Detect). | Mark the function where your last team was weakest and write why.
SME Question: An executive asks which framework you would use for a 200-person SaaS startup and why. Answer in 90 seconds.

Name: Day 04: Build your home lab with Docker
Outcome: Run an isolated, disposable lab with vulnerable apps and an attacker toolbox.
Lab: Read labs/LAB_SETUP.md, then run `docker compose -f labs/docker-compose.yml up -d`. | Open Juice Shop on http://localhost:3000 and DVWA on http://localhost:8081, and confirm both load. | Exec into the attacker box: `docker compose -f labs/docker-compose.yml exec attacker bash`, then `curl -I http://juice-shop:3000`. | Run `docker compose -f labs/docker-compose.yml ps` and confirm every published port is bound to 127.0.0.1 only. Write down why that matters.
SME Question: Why must vulnerable lab targets never be exposed on a public IP, and how did you enforce that?
Deliverable: notes/day-04.md with a screenshot or the output proving the lab works.

Name: Day 05: Linux command line for security, part 1
Outcome: Move around Linux, read files in awkward ways, and use ssh comfortably under pressure.
Lab: Play Bandit levels 0 to 6. | For each level, record the command that solved it and the concept (hidden files, spaces in names, file types). | Never store the passwords themselves in the repo; store the technique.
SME Question: How would you find every file on a server owned by user X, of size 33 bytes, that is not executable?

Name: Day 06: Linux command line for security, part 2
Outcome: Use find, grep, sort, uniq, base64, tr and tar/gzip to dig through data fast.
Lab: Play Bandit levels 7 to 13. | Note how ROT13, hexdump and nested compression show up and which tool decoded each. | Write a one-line shell alias you would add to your attacker box after today.
SME Question: Why do attackers and defenders both live in the shell? Give two tasks where grep beats a GUI.

Name: Day 07: Week 1 review and checkpoint
Outcome: Explain week 1 concepts without notes and fill your gaps.
Lab: Answer the week 1 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud, and record yourself on your phone. | Rate yourself 1-5 on each day in the tracker and redo the lowest one. | Stretch: Bandit levels 14-16 (netcat, openssl s_client).
SME Question: Teach CIA, risk and the CSF to a non-technical friend in 3 minutes.
Deliverable: notes/week-01-review.md with your confidence ratings and gaps.

Name: Day 08: OSI and TCP/IP models, TCP handshake
Outcome: Walk through encapsulation layer by layer and spot a TCP three-way handshake in a capture.
Lab: In the attacker container: `tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/day08.pcap port 3000` in one shell. | In another shell run `curl http://juice-shop:3000`, then stop the capture. | Read it back with `tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/day08.pcap` and label SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, data and FIN.
SME Question: What happens at each layer when you type a URL and press Enter, and where can an attacker interfere?

Name: Day 09: IP addressing, subnets, NAT and ports
Outcome: Subnet quickly, explain NAT, and know the 20 most common ports and what runs on them.
Lab: Do 10 subnetting questions until you can answer each in under 60 seconds. | Run `ss -tulpn` on your machine and in the lab containers and map each listening port to a service. | Write the common ports table from memory (22, 25, 53, 80, 88, 135, 139, 389, 443, 445, 636, 1433, 3306, 3389, 5432, 5985, 6379, 8080, 9200, 27017), then check it.
SME Question: Why is 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 in a security group a finding, and what would you replace it with?

Name: Day 10: DNS and HTTP through a security lens
Outcome: Trace a DNS resolution, read every part of an HTTP request and response, and name DNS attacks.
Lab: `dig +trace example.com` and label root, TLD and authoritative servers. | `dig example.com TXT`, `dig example.com MX` and explain what each record is used for. | `curl -v https://example.com` and label the method, status code, headers and cookies. | Write two lines each on DNS spoofing/cache poisoning, DNS tunnelling and subdomain takeover.
SME Question: How can DNS be used to exfiltrate data, and how would you detect it?

Name: Day 11: Packet analysis with Wireshark
Outcome: Filter, follow streams and pull evidence (credentials, files, hostnames) out of a pcap.
Lab: Install Wireshark on your host machine. | Download a plain-text protocol capture (HTTP or FTP or Telnet) from the sample captures page. | Use display filters: `http.request`, `ftp`, `tcp.stream eq 0`, `dns.qry.name contains`. | Use Follow TCP Stream to recover the cleartext credentials or content, then write what control would have prevented it.
SME Question: A pcap from a breach lands on your desk. What are the first five filters you apply and why?
Deliverable: notes/day-11.md with your filters cheat sheet.

Name: Day 12: Network reconnaissance with Nmap
Outcome: Choose the right Nmap scan for the job and interpret open, closed and filtered results.
Lab: From the attacker container: `nmap -sn 172.30.0.0/24` to find hosts on the lab network. | `nmap -sV -sC -p- juice-shop dvwa` and record services and versions. | Compare a SYN scan (-sS) and a connect scan (-sT) and note the difference in your own words. | Only scan your lab or scanme.nmap.org, which Nmap explicitly allows. Scanning anything else needs written permission.
SME Question: Why can a port show as 'filtered', and what does that tell you about the network?

Name: Day 13: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, segmentation and zero trust
Outcome: Explain stateful firewalls, WAFs, IDS vs IPS, segmentation and the core zero trust tenets.
Lab: In a throwaway Ubuntu container or VM, install nftables or ufw. | Default-deny inbound, allow only 22 from one IP, and allow established traffic. | Prove it with nmap from the attacker box before and after. | Write the rule set and the evidence into your notes.
SME Question: What does 'never trust, always verify' change compared with a VPN plus flat network?

Name: Day 14: Week 2 review and checkpoint
Outcome: Draw a packet's journey with every security control on the path.
Lab: Draw (draw.io or paper) a browser to database request: DNS, CDN/WAF, load balancer, firewall, app, DB. | Mark where TLS terminates, where logs are produced and where an attacker could sit. | Answer the week 2 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud.
SME Question: Walk an interviewer through that diagram in 3 minutes.

Name: Day 15: Linux hardening and logging
Outcome: Audit and harden a Linux host, and know where its security logs live.
Lab: In an Ubuntu container, install and run `lynis audit system`, and note the hardening index. | Find SUID binaries: `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`. | Harden sshd_config (no root login, no passwords, modern ciphers) and explain each line. | Look at /var/log/auth.log (or `journalctl -u ssh`) and find failed logins. | Re-run Lynis and record the new score.
SME Question: Give the five Linux hardening steps you would bake into every base image and why.

Name: Day 16: Windows security fundamentals
Outcome: Explain Windows accounts, UAC, the registry, and the event IDs every analyst knows.
Lab: Complete the TryHackMe room (it gives you a browser-based Windows VM). | Learn these event IDs and write one line each: 4624, 4625, 4634, 4648, 4672, 4688, 4720, 4732, 1102, 7045. | Note what Sysmon adds over the default logs (process command lines, network connections, hashes).
SME Question: Which Windows events would show a brute-force attack followed by a successful login and a new admin user?
Deliverable: notes/day-16.md with your event ID table.

Name: Day 17: Active Directory and Kerberos basics
Outcome: Explain domains, OUs, GPOs, Kerberos tickets and the classic AD attacks at concept level.
Lab: Complete the TryHackMe room. | Draw the Kerberos flow (AS-REQ, TGT, TGS-REQ, service ticket). | Write one paragraph each on Kerberoasting, pass-the-hash and Golden Ticket, and the defence for each.
SME Question: Why is Active Directory the first thing attackers go after in a corporate network?

Name: Day 18: Authentication, passwords, MFA and passkeys
Outcome: Explain modern password guidance, how passwords should be stored, and why phishing-resistant MFA matters.
Lab: Create 5 test passwords of your own (weak and strong), hash them with MD5 and bcrypt using Python. | Crack the MD5 ones with hashcat or john and a small wordlist, then try the bcrypt ones and time it. | Write down why salting and slow hashes changed the outcome.
SME Question: Why are SMS codes weaker than passkeys, and what is MFA fatigue?

Name: Day 19: Authorization, IAM and least privilege
Outcome: Compare RBAC and ABAC, write least-privilege policies, and explain privileged access management.
Lab: Take an over-broad IAM policy (s3:* on *) and rewrite it to read one bucket prefix only. | Write a Kubernetes Role and RoleBinding that only lets a CI service account update one Deployment. | List three ways a role can be escalated (iam:PassRole, wildcard actions, bind/escalate verbs in RBAC).
SME Question: What is least privilege, and how do you actually achieve it at scale without slowing engineers down?

Name: Day 20: Federation with OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML and JWT
Outcome: Explain the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE, how OIDC adds identity, and common JWT mistakes.
Lab: Create a free PortSwigger account and solve the first JWT lab (unverified signature). | Decode a JWT and explain header, payload and signature. | Write the 5 steps of the authorization code flow with PKCE from memory.
SME Question: What is the difference between OAuth and OIDC, and when would you still pick SAML?

Name: Day 21: Week 3 review and checkpoint
Outcome: Defend a host and an identity design in front of a reviewer.
Lab: Answer the week 3 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud. | Write a one-page 'identity standard' for a company (MFA, SSO, joiner/mover/leaver, break-glass accounts).
SME Question: An attacker steals a developer laptop. Walk through which identity controls limit the damage.

Name: Day 22: Symmetric and asymmetric crypto, key exchange
Outcome: Explain AES, block modes, RSA/ECC and Diffie-Hellman, and when each is used.
Lab: Encrypt and decrypt a file with `openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -salt`. Note that `openssl enc` cannot do AEAD modes like GCM, which is one reason apps use crypto libraries instead. | Generate an Ed25519 and an RSA key with `openssl genpkey` and compare sizes. | In CyberChef, encrypt the same text with AES-ECB and AES-CBC and see why ECB leaks patterns.
SME Question: Why does TLS use asymmetric crypto to agree a key and then switch to symmetric crypto?

Name: Day 23: Hashing, MACs and digital signatures
Outcome: Distinguish hash, HMAC and signature, and sign and verify artifacts.
Lab: `sha256sum` a file, change one byte and compare (avalanche effect). | Create an HMAC with `openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac`. | Sign a file with your Ed25519 key and verify it, then tamper with the file and verify again. | Optional: sign a container image with `cosign sign-blob` or `cosign sign`.
SME Question: Why is a hash on a download page not enough to prove the file came from the vendor?

Name: Day 24: PKI and TLS
Outcome: Read a certificate chain, explain the TLS 1.3 handshake and debug common TLS failures.
Lab: `openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -showcerts` and identify leaf, intermediate and root. | Look up a domain you know on crt.sh (https://crt.sh/) and explain Certificate Transparency. | Run the Qualys SSL Labs test (https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/) on a site you own or a big public site. | Create a local CA, issue a server cert and a client cert, and describe how mTLS uses them.
SME Question: A service throws 'certificate verify failed'. List five possible causes in order of likelihood.

Name: Day 25: Secrets management and crypto failures
Outcome: Explain why secrets leak, how to rotate them, and run a secrets manager and a secrets scanner.
Lab: Run Vault in dev mode: `docker run --rm -p 8200:8200 hashicorp/vault`, then write and read a KV secret. | Make a scratch git repo, commit a fake AWS key, delete it in a second commit, then run gitleaks and find it. | Write the 4-step response to a real leaked key (revoke, rotate, investigate usage, prevent).
SME Question: Why is deleting a leaked secret from git not enough?

Name: Day 26: Browser security model and security headers
Outcome: Explain same-origin policy, CORS, cookie flags and the main security headers.
Lab: Scan two public sites with the HTTP Observatory and compare grades. | In browser dev tools, inspect cookies on a site and note Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite. | Write the header set you would ship by default (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy).
SME Question: CORS is not a security control that protects your server. Explain why.

Name: Day 27: OWASP Top 10 overview and Burp Suite
Outcome: Name the OWASP Top 10 categories and intercept, modify and replay requests in Burp.
Lab: Install Burp Suite Community and use its built-in browser. | Browse Juice Shop through Burp, send a login request to Repeater and change parameters. | Find the Juice Shop score board (hint, it is a hidden route) and solve one 1-star challenge.
SME Question: Pick three OWASP Top 10 categories and give a real-world breach for each.

Name: Day 28: Week 4 review and checkpoint
Outcome: Explain crypto and web basics with confidence and fix your weakest topic.
Lab: Answer the week 4 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud. | Explain the TLS handshake on a whiteboard in under 2 minutes, and record it. | Stretch: Cryptopals set 1, challenges 1-3.
SME Question: Explain end-to-end encryption vs encryption in transit vs encryption at rest.

Name: Day 29: SQL injection
Outcome: Find and exploit SQLi in labs, and fix it with parameterised queries.
Lab: Solve the first two PortSwigger SQLi apprentice labs (WHERE clause and login bypass). | Solve the DVWA SQL Injection page at Low security. | Rewrite the vulnerable query in your favourite language using a parameterised query.
SME Question: Why do parameterised queries fix SQLi when input escaping often fails?

Name: Day 30: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
Outcome: Explain reflected, stored and DOM XSS, exploit each in labs, and prevent them with encoding and CSP.
Lab: Solve the reflected and stored XSS apprentice labs on PortSwigger. | Solve the Juice Shop 'DOM XSS' challenge. | Write a CSP that would have blocked your payload, and explain which directive did it.
SME Question: If cookies are HttpOnly, is XSS still dangerous? Explain.

Name: Day 31: Broken access control and IDOR
Outcome: Find horizontal and vertical privilege escalation and explain server-side authorization checks.
Lab: Solve two access control apprentice labs (unprotected admin, user ID in request parameter). | In Juice Shop, view another user's basket by changing an ID in Burp. | Write the code-level fix (check ownership on the server for every object access).
SME Question: Why has broken access control been the number one OWASP risk, and why can scanners rarely find it?

Name: Day 32: Authentication flaws, sessions and CSRF
Outcome: Attack weak login and session handling in labs and explain CSRF and its defences.
Lab: Solve the username enumeration via different responses lab. | Solve the CSRF vulnerability with no defences lab. | Note how SameSite=Lax cookies change the CSRF picture.
SME Question: How do SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and re-authentication each reduce CSRF risk?

Name: Day 33: SSRF, command injection and path traversal
Outcome: Exploit server-side injection classes in labs and explain why SSRF is critical in the cloud.
Lab: Solve one apprentice lab in each of SSRF, OS command injection and path traversal. | Read about how SSRF to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) leads to stolen IAM credentials. | Write why IMDSv2 (session tokens, hop limit) mitigates it.
SME Question: Walk through how an SSRF bug can turn into a full AWS account compromise, and the three controls that break the chain.

Name: Day 34: API security
Outcome: Explain the OWASP API Security Top 10 and test an API for BOLA and mass assignment.
Lab: Solve the PortSwigger 'exploiting an API endpoint using documentation' lab. | In Juice Shop, use the REST API through Burp to read or change data you should not have access to. | Map each finding to an OWASP API Top 10 item.
SME Question: Why are APIs a bigger attack surface than the web UI built on top of them?

Name: Day 35: Week 5 review and secure code review
Outcome: Spot vulnerabilities in code and explain the fix like an AppSec engineer.
Lab: Pick 3 Juice Shop challenges you solved and find the vulnerable line in the Juice Shop source on GitHub. | Write a short PR-style comment for each with the risk and the fix. | Answer the week 5 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud.
SME Question: A developer says 'the framework handles security'. Respond with two examples where it does not.

Name: Day 36: Ethics, rules of engagement and pentest methodology
Outcome: Explain legal boundaries, scoping and the phases of a penetration test and the kill chain.
Lab: Write a one-page rules of engagement for testing your own lab (scope, out of scope, timing, contacts, data handling). | Map the pentest phases (planning, recon, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting) to what you have done so far.
SME Question: What is the difference between a vulnerability scan, a penetration test and a red team exercise?

Name: Day 37: MITRE ATT&CK
Outcome: Navigate ATT&CK, map a real intrusion to techniques, and use it to find detection gaps.
Lab: Pick a public incident report (for example a CISA advisory) and list the techniques used with their T-IDs. | Create a Navigator layer, colour those techniques and export the JSON into labs/attack/. | Mark which ones you could detect with logs you have seen so far.
SME Question: How would you use ATT&CK to tell a CISO where the detection gaps are?

Name: Day 38: Vulnerability management, CVE, CVSS, EPSS and KEV
Outcome: Score and prioritise vulnerabilities using severity, exploitability and exposure, not just CVSS.
Lab: Scan an old image: `docker run --rm aquasec/trivy image python:3.8`. | Pick 3 critical CVEs from the output, check their EPSS score and whether they are in KEV. | Rank them and justify the order in one paragraph.
SME Question: You have 4,000 open vulnerabilities and one sprint. How do you decide what to fix?

Name: Day 39: Exploitation basics and Metasploit
Outcome: Explain payloads, bind vs reverse shells and run a controlled exploit in a lab.
Lab: Complete the TryHackMe room. | In your lab, catch a reverse shell from the DVWA command injection page to the attacker container with netcat. | Write which egress control would have stopped the reverse shell.
SME Question: Why do attackers prefer reverse shells, and how does egress filtering help defenders?

Name: Day 40: Linux privilege escalation
Outcome: Enumerate a Linux box for privilege escalation paths and know the defence for each.
Lab: Work through the first tasks of the room (sudo, SUID, cron, PATH). | For each technique you used, write the hardening setting that prevents it.
SME Question: A developer has sudo on vim in production. Why is that a full root compromise?

Name: Day 41: Phishing, email security and password attacks
Outcome: Analyse a phishing email and explain SPF, DKIM, DMARC, password spraying and credential stuffing.
Lab: `dig TXT gmail.com`, `dig TXT _dmarc.gmail.com` and explain each record. | Open the raw headers of a spam email in your own inbox and trace the Received chain and auth results. | Write the red flags and the verdict like a SOC analyst would.
SME Question: Why does DMARC with p=reject matter, and why can phishing still land in inboxes?

Name: Day 42: Week 6 review and mini pentest report
Outcome: Communicate findings in a report a developer can fix and an executive can understand.
Lab: Write a mini report on your Juice Shop/DVWA findings using labs/templates/pentest-report.md. | Include an executive summary, three findings with CVSS, evidence and remediation. | Answer the week 6 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud.
SME Question: Present your top finding to a CTO in 2 minutes with business impact.

Name: Day 43: Security logging and SIEM fundamentals
Outcome: Explain what to log, how a SIEM normalises and correlates data, and investigate raw logs.
Lab: Export the Juice Shop container logs and your Ubuntu auth.log from earlier labs. | Using grep, awk and jq, answer which IP made the most failed logins and when the first suspicious request happened. | Write which fields a good security log must have (who, what, when, where, outcome).
SME Question: Logging everything is expensive. How do you decide what goes into the SIEM?

Name: Day 44: Detection engineering with Sigma
Outcome: Write a Sigma rule, convert it to a SIEM query and treat detections as code.
Lab: Write a Sigma rule that detects 10 failed SSH logins from one IP in 5 minutes. | Install sigma-cli with pip and convert your rule and one rule from the repo to a backend query. | Add the rule to detections/ and describe how you would unit test it in CI.
SME Question: What makes a detection good? Talk about true positives, false positives, coverage and maintenance.

Name: Day 45: Incident response lifecycle
Outcome: Lead an incident through preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
Lab: Write a playbook for 'AWS access key leaked on GitHub' using labs/templates/ir-playbook.md. | Include triage questions, containment steps, evidence to collect (CloudTrail), communication and recovery. | Time-box a 10-minute tabletop with yourself, walking through the playbook as if it were real.
SME Question: Contain or investigate first? Explain the trade-off with an example.

Name: Day 46: Digital forensics and traffic analysis
Outcome: Explain order of volatility and chain of custody, and analyse a malicious traffic capture.
Lab: Pick a beginner exercise from malware-traffic-analysis.net (pcaps are password-protected zips; analyse only in your lab VM). | Identify the infected host, its hostname and the suspicious domains or IPs. | Write a short incident summary with IOCs.
SME Question: What is the order of volatility and why does it matter in the first hour of an incident?

Name: Day 47: Malware basics, threat intelligence and YARA
Outcome: Explain malware families, IOCs vs TTPs, the Pyramid of Pain, and write a YARA rule.
Lab: Install YARA (`apt install yara` or `pip install yara-python`). | Write a rule that matches a fake 'malware' text file you create with specific strings and a condition. | Test it against a folder of mixed files and record matches.
SME Question: Why are TTPs more valuable than hashes and IP addresses for defenders?

Name: Day 48: Threat hunting and purple teaming
Outcome: Run a hypothesis-driven hunt and test a detection with an Atomic Red Team test.
Lab: Write a hunt hypothesis, for example 'an attacker added persistence via cron on a Linux host'. | Simulate it in your Ubuntu container (add a cron job) using the matching Atomic test as a guide (T1053.003). | Find it with commands or logs, then write a detection for it.
SME Question: What is the difference between detection and hunting, and how does purple teaming connect them?

Name: Day 49: Week 7 review and tabletop exercise
Outcome: Run a tabletop and explain the SOC workflow end to end.
Lab: Pick one CISA tabletop scenario and answer its discussion questions for your imagined company. | Answer the week 7 questions in sme/INTERVIEW_QUESTIONS.md out loud.
SME Question: Walk through an alert from the SIEM to a closed incident with lessons learned.

Name: Day 50: Cloud security fundamentals
Outcome: Explain the shared responsibility model and the top cloud misconfigurations.
Lab: Solve flAWS levels 1 and 2 (public S3 bucket and authenticated-users misconfiguration). | For each level, write the misconfiguration, the impact and the fix.
SME Question: Who is responsible for a data leak from a public S3 bucket, and why?

Name: Day 51: AWS security services and cloud detection
Outcome: Explain CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub, SCPs and how to investigate in AWS.
Lab: Solve flAWS levels 3 and 4 (secrets in git history, public snapshots). | If you have a personal AWS account: run Prowler with read-only credentials and review the top 10 failed checks. | Write a CloudTrail query (Athena or CLI) that finds who created an access key in the last 24 hours.
SME Question: An IAM key was used from an unusual country. What do you check, in what order?

Name: Day 52: Container security
Outcome: Harden images and runtime, and explain container escape risks.
Lab: Take a naive Dockerfile (root user, full OS base, secrets in ENV) and harden it (non-root, distroless or slim, multi-stage, no secrets). | Scan both images with Trivy and compare counts. | Run Docker Bench on your host and fix two findings.
SME Question: Why is mounting the Docker socket into a container equivalent to giving root on the host?
Deliverable: labs/container-hardening/ with both Dockerfiles and results.

Name: Day 53: Kubernetes security
Outcome: Secure a cluster with RBAC, Pod Security Standards, network policies and secrets handling.
Lab: Create a cluster with kind (https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/). | Label a namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted and try deploying a privileged pod. | Add a default-deny NetworkPolicy and prove it blocks traffic (kind needs a CNI such as Calico for policies). | Run kube-bench as a Job and review the failures.
SME Question: Name five things you check first when reviewing a Kubernetes cluster's security.

Name: Day 54: CI/CD and software supply chain security
Outcome: Explain the OWASP CI/CD Top 10, SLSA, SBOMs and how to harden GitHub Actions.
Lab: Generate an SBOM for a container image with syft (https://github.com/anchore/syft). | Review a GitHub Actions workflow you know for pull_request_target misuse, unpinned actions and over-broad GITHUB_TOKEN permissions. | Fix it (pin actions by SHA, set permissions to read-only by default, use OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys).
SME Question: Explain the SolarWinds or the tj-actions/changed-files compromise and the controls that would have limited it.

Name: Day 55: AppSec tooling in the pipeline (SAST, SCA, DAST, IaC, secrets)
Outcome: Build a security pipeline and explain what each tool class finds and misses.
Lab: Add .github/workflows/devsecops-demo.yml to a scratch repo with semgrep, gitleaks, checkov and trivy steps. | Add a deliberately bad Terraform file (public S3 bucket) and a vulnerable code snippet and watch the jobs fail. | Run a ZAP baseline scan against your local Juice Shop.
SME Question: A team complains the security scanners block every PR with noise. How do you fix that without losing coverage?
Deliverable: labs/devsecops-pipeline/ with the workflow and results.

Name: Day 56: Threat modeling
Outcome: Run a STRIDE threat model on a data flow diagram and turn threats into backlog items.
Lab: Draw a data flow diagram of a CI/CD pipeline deploying to Kubernetes, with trust boundaries. | Apply STRIDE to each element and list at least 8 threats. | Rank them and write mitigations as user stories.
SME Question: What are the four questions of threat modeling, and when in the SDLC should it happen?

Name: Day 57: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC)
Outcome: Explain risk treatment, policies vs standards vs procedures, and what ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS and GDPR require.
Lab: Write a one-page access control policy and a matching standard (specific settings) and procedure (steps). | Map three of your earlier labs to SOC 2 or ISO 27001 controls as audit evidence. | List the four risk treatments (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid) with an example each.
SME Question: Compliant is not the same as secure. Explain with an example.

Name: Day 58: Security architecture and secure design principles
Outcome: Design a secure cloud architecture using defence in depth and secure design principles.
Lab: Design a 3-tier web app on AWS (or your cloud) and draw it. | Annotate identity, network, data protection, logging/detection and incident response controls. | Note which design principle (least privilege, fail secure, defence in depth, separation of duties) each control follows.
SME Question: Defend your architecture against a reviewer who asks 'what happens if the web tier is compromised?'

Name: Day 59: Capstone, attack, detect, respond, fix
Outcome: Prove the fundamentals end to end in one exercise you can show in interviews.
Lab: Follow capstone/CAPSTONE.md. Exploit one Juice Shop vulnerability (SQLi login bypass). | Find the attack in the logs and write the detection. | Write a short incident report and a remediation (code fix or WAF rule plus pipeline check).
SME Question: Present the capstone in 5 minutes as if to a hiring panel.

Name: Day 60: SME readiness, mock interview and next 90 days
